<reason>Side B (PRO) won the decisive clash. CON's strongest escape—answering catastrophic healthcare with subsidized insurance—was turned into a concession by PRO's sharpest move: insurance is earmarked, pooled, restricted spending, i.e., the proposition's principle wearing CON's label, and it is not unconditional cash. CON's counter that insurance is not government-operated in-kind provision had some force, but PRO's supply-side argument was never neutralized: cash cannot summon a daycare, bus route, or specialist into a thin market, and extra purchasing power there just bids up prices. CON's "wrong zip code" worry was answered with siting/radius and the asymmetry that underused infrastructure is correctable while a family priced out of a nonexistent supply cannot fix anything with a check. PRO's closing weighing—markets working favors neither, markets failing favors only services, and high fixed costs/thin supply are the ordinary shape of these needs—gave the cleaner decision rule, blunting CON's "retreat to a narrow case" framing. CON performed well: the heterogeneity/rigidity line, the sewers-vs-childcare natural monopoly distinction, and "a bad bus route lasts decades" were all real contributions, and both sides executed the Q/A format cleanly. But CON left the desert-supply and price-inflation points substantially unanswered and leaned on assertion ("existing systems are famous for rigidity") where PRO offered mechanisms. Grounding was honest on both sides with no fake sourcing; PRO's epistemic discipline and crystallization were slightly superior.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1–B4.3: PRO's answer to the insurance pressure question—"insurance is money that is earmarked, pooled, and spent on a defined service... you cannot use a premium to fix your roof"—converted CON's escape hatch into a concession of the motion's core principle, then paired it with "insurance cannot pay out a daycare that doesn't exist" to close the loop: pooling solves risk, only provision solves missing supply.</best_rebuttal>
